d.title: Nothing in the objective mentions a question or an answer
d.caption: Everything a base model knows arrives through one expression: cross-entropy on the next token, averaged over the corpus. **No question, no instruction, no answer, no user appears in it anywhere** — which is the entire reason the rest of this module exists. What it produces at inference is a probability distribution over next tokens, and nothing about that distribution knows it is supposed to be helpful.

nodes.label: No question, no answer, no user
nodes.sub: none of it is in the loss

nodes.label: And nothing about being helpful
nodes.sub: which is the rest of this module

d.title: A base model asked four questions, and what it actually did
d.caption: It continued the document. *What is the capital of France?* produced **"The capital of France is Paris." four times over** — the fact is there and the format is a loop. *Write a polite email declining a meeting* produced dialogue from a novel. And the token distribution explains all of it: **33.84% of the next-token mass is on a newline**, because in the training corpus a question is usually followed by more document, not by an answer. `' Paris'` gets 0.54%.

steps.code: What is the capital of France?

d.title: Two relations, and the worked example that checks them
d.caption: Once the objective is fixed the only decisions left are **how big the model is and how much text it sees**, and those trade under a compute budget. Two relations answer it: training FLOPs ≈ 6ND, and compute-optimal D ≈ 20N. The 6 is roughly 2 for the forward pass and 4 for the backward, per parameter per token. Worked through for a 7B model the arithmetic reproduces the published figure exactly.

d.title: Llama-3 8B is 93.8x past compute-optimal, deliberately
d.caption: Chinchilla answers: given a fixed **training** budget, what size and token count minimise loss? That is the right question for a lab publishing a result and the wrong one for a product, because **a served model runs billions of times after training ends**. So Llama-3 8B saw ~15T tokens — **1,875 tokens per parameter against the optimal 20** — spending 93.8× the training compute to get a smaller model that is cheaper to serve forever.

d.title: Where the remaining variance actually lives
d.caption: The claim practitioners confirm most consistently is that **data mix and deduplication beat almost every architectural tweak**. That is not a claim that transformers are perfect — it is a claim about where the variance is left: the architecture has been optimised by thousands of people against public benchmarks, and your corpus has not. Which is also why this is the stage a product team can affect and the rest of it is not.

nodes.label: That is where the variance is
And it is what you control

d.title: The same loss, with most positions masked out
d.caption: SFT is ordinary cross-entropy on `(prompt, response)` pairs — **no new mathematics**. What changes is that the data now has structure: part of each sequence is input to condition on and part is output to learn. **Cross-entropy does not know the difference**, so handing it the concatenated sequence supervises every position, training the model to generate prompts too. The mask is what makes it SFT rather than more pretraining.

d.title: A chat template is structural, not cosmetic
d.caption: 7.1 measured a base model putting **33.84% of its next-token mass on a newline** after a question — it had no representation of a turn *ending*. A chat template supplies that representation: special tokens that mean "the user's part stops here" and "your part stops here". Which is why using the wrong template at inference is not a formatting preference — the model was trained to recognise specific tokens, and different ones leave it without the boundary it learned to depend on.

nodes.label: A base model has no turn boundary
So the model knows when to stop
nodes.sub: and when it is being addressed

nodes.label: Use a different template at inference

d.title: Three orders of magnitude, and what each is actually buying
d.caption: The reason the numbers differ by so much is in the right-hand column rather than in the task's difficulty. **100–1,000 teaches a surface pattern the model can already produce** — you are selecting among behaviours it has, not installing one. Behaviour across varied inputs needs coverage of the variation, which is why the middle row is ten times the first. And the last row is what a lab builds, not a product team.
cells: a surface pattern it can already produce
behaviour needs coverage of the variation
the whole repertoire - what a lab builds

d.title: The scores are a latent construct invented to fit the clicks
d.caption: You want a function saying this answer is worth 7.2 and that one 3.1, and **humans cannot supply that** — ask ten people to rate an answer out of ten and you get ten different scales. They *can* reliably say A is better than B. So you collect comparisons and fit a scalar model whose **differences** explain them. Which is why the absolute scale means nothing: it was never measured, only inferred, and any constant added to every score fits the data equally well.

nodes.label: Ask for a score out of ten
Fit a scalar whose differences fit
So the absolute scale means nothing

d.title: Three cases, and the asymmetry in the penalty
d.caption: The loss is −log σ(gap). When the model has a preference **backwards** — a gap of −1.3 — the loss is 1.5410, which is **3.5× the penalty** of merely being unconfident at +0.6. And when it is already confident at +4.0 the loss is 0.0181, essentially nothing. That shape is the design: being wrong is expensive, being right is cheap, and being *more* right than necessary is free — which §03 shows is also the weakness.

d.title: Saturation: the gradient is 1 - sigma(gap)
d.caption: The gradient has an unusually clean closed form, and reading it down the table is the whole of 7.11 in advance. At a gap of 0 the gradient is at **50% of maximum**; at a gap of 4 it is **1.8%**; at 8 it is zero to four decimal places. So once the model has a comfortable margin on a pair, **nothing constrains how much larger that margin becomes** — there is no force pulling it back, which is precisely the room reward hacking exploits.

d.title: 78.6% is not the reward model failing — it is the ceiling
d.caption: Held-out preference accuracy is the right metric, and below about 65% downstream RL chases noise. What the usual framing leaves out is that **the ceiling is not 100%**. Fitted on its own training pairs the model reaches 78.6% — and computing the **Bayes-optimal** accuracy using the *true* rewards gives **78.6% as well**. The preference data is stochastic, so a perfect reward model would also be wrong 21.4% of the time, and chasing that gap is chasing label noise.

steps.code: fitted RM on its training pairs

d.title: A reward model is the SFT model with its head replaced
d.caption: The construction is simpler than it sounds: take the SFT model, replace the language-modelling head with **a single scalar output**, and train it on the pairwise loss. It starts from a model that already understands the domain, so it is learning a ranking rather than learning language. The practical consequences follow: it costs an extra model in memory during PPO, and it inherits whatever the SFT model was good and bad at.

nodes.label: And it inherits the SFT model's gaps

d.title: Two terms, and the leash is folded into the reward
d.caption: The first term says **get a high score from the reward model**; the second says **do not drift far from the frozen SFT model**, with β — typically 0.01 to 0.1 — setting the leash length. In practice the KL is not a separate objective term at all: it is folded into the per-token reward, so the sequence reward arrives only on the last token and every other token's reward is purely the KL penalty. Which is why the advantage estimate needs a critic.

nodes.label: The sequence reward is on the last token
So a critic has to estimate the rest

d.title: The clipping gloss is right for positive advantages and wrong in general
d.caption: "If this update would move a token's probability more than ±20%, stop giving credit for going further" is the usual explanation, and the arithmetic shows it is only half the story. With a **negative** advantage the `min` picks the *unclipped* term — so at ρ = 2.0 and A = −1 the objective is −2.000, not the clipped −1.200. **Clipping limits how much you reward a move and does not limit how much you punish one.** That asymmetry is deliberate: a bad action should be discouraged however far the policy has already drifted.

d.title: One step in the loop is not a forward pass
d.caption: Every stage of PPO is a forward or backward pass over a batch — **except step 1, which is autoregressive generation**, one token at a time, and module 3 established that is memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound. So it dominates the wall clock and attracts all the engineering: a separate inference-optimised copy of the policy, continuous batching, KV caching. **DPO has no generation in its loop at all**, which is the second reason it displaced PPO for most teams.

nodes.label: Step 1: generate completions
nodes.sub: autoregressive, one token at a time

d.title: Three steps, and nothing is approximated
d.caption: The derivation is worth following because it explains why DPO needs no reward model rather than merely asserting it. The KL-constrained objective has a **known optimum** — the reference policy tilted exponentially toward high reward. Take logs and solve for the reward: pure algebra. Substitute into the Bradley-Terry loss, which depends only on the **difference** of two rewards for the same prompt — and since `Z(x)` depends only on `x`, it is identical in both terms and **cancels**. The intractable partition function disappears for free.

items.desc: the reference policy, exponentially tilted toward reward

d.title: The implicit reward, worked on real log-probabilities
d.caption: There is no reward model, and there is still a reward: **β times the log-ratio against the reference**. The chosen response's policy log-prob is 1.0 above its reference, giving an implicit reward of 0.10 at β = 0.1; the rejected one is 0.5 above, giving 0.05. The margin is **0.05**, and the loss is −log σ(0.05) = 0.6685 — barely below −log σ(0) = 0.693, which is the honest reading: this pair is almost unseparated and the gradient will be near its maximum.

d.title: Beta scales the margin, so it scales the effective learning rate
d.caption: β multiplies the log-ratio, so it multiplies the margin and therefore moves where you sit on §02's sigmoid. At **β = 0.01 the margin is 0.0050 and the gradient is 0.4988 — essentially the maximum**, so every pair is treated as unseparated and the model is pushed hard on all of them. At β = 1.0 the margin is 0.5 and the gradient has fallen to 0.3775. Which reframes β: it is described as the KL leash, and mechanically it is also a gain on the gradient.

d.title: Four models or two, and the row that is not about memory
d.caption: PPO holds four models — **234.7 GB at 7B** — against DPO's two at 117.3 GB, or one with LoRA. But the row that decides architecture rather than hardware is the second-to-last: **PPO can exceed its data**, because it samples and explores beyond the preference set, and DPO cannot. That is the real reason frontier labs still run PPO for reasoning work while everyone else uses DPO. Note also the learning rate: **~5e-7, much lower than SFT**, and getting that wrong is a common first failure.
